steps.prompt: Write the move you chose, and what you think could stop it. Nothing is explained yet.

steps.text: **Double check** means one move gives check twice, so the king has to move. After this lesson you can do four things: **see** one coming, **judge** whether it works (and when the king simply takes the checking piece), **set one up** or stop one against you, and **tell** a real double check from a look-alike. First, boards from easy to hard: watch what the first move does.

steps.caption: The hook position again, Black to move. The queen on h2 looks along the second rank at the king on a2, but Black's own bishop on c2 stands in the way.

line.say: The bishop steps off the rank and attacks the king itself, while the queen's line opens: two checks at once.
White cannot capture or block two checkers, so the king must move.
The queen takes the open rank. The bishop protects her: checkmate.

After the bishop moves, two black pieces attack the king on a2.
Black forces mate within two moves.

The king moves. One of its three squares.

steps.text: **Two pieces on one line.** Every board had the same parts. A *back piece* (a queen, rook or bishop) aims at the king along a line, and a *front piece* stands in the way. When the front piece moves, the back piece gives check. If the front piece also gives check from its new square, that is a **double check**. So the search is: find a piece standing between your long-range piece and the enemy king.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen on e5 aims at the king on h8, but White's rook on f6 stands on that diagonal. A harder one: the front piece is a rook that captures.

line.say: The rook takes a pawn and checks down the h-file. The diagonal opens: two checks.
The queen takes the black queen with mate.

claims.statement: The rook capture is legal.
After the rook captures, two white pieces attack the king on h8.
White forces mate within two moves.
This move is the engine's first choice (depth 16).

steps.text: **Remember.** A double check is one move that gives check twice, so the king must move. Look for a front piece standing between your long-range piece and the enemy king. When it moves and also gives check, you have it. Judge it first: ask whether the king can simply take the checking piece. Scan for the same pattern against you.
